title: Cardiac Damage Biomarkers and Heart Rate Variability Following a 118-Km Mountain Race: Relationship with Performance and Recovery
authors: Martinez-Navarro I, Sanchez-Gomez JM, Collado-Boira EJ, Hernando B, Panizo N, Hernando C
journal: Journal of Sports Science and Medicine
population: 46 athletes in the Penyagolosa Trails CSP115 race (118 km, 5439 m positive elevation), measured before and after the race
findings: High-sensitive troponin T exceeded the upper reference limit in 50% of finishers and NT-proBNP in 87%.
Overall and vagally mediated HRV were diminished and cardiac autonomic modulation became less complex and more predictable after the race.

More pronounced vagal modulation decreases were associated with higher post-exertional NT-proBNP; the rise in hs-TNT and NT-proBNP was greater among faster runners, and pre-race HRV correlated with finishing time.

Authors conclude an appropriate recovery period after ultra-endurance races appears prudent, particularly for better-performing athletes, and that HRV is a promising tool to assess readiness to perform at maximum level in an ultra-endurance race.
limitations: Only pre and post measurement, no follow-up days, so it does not date any return to normal; no DOI exists in PubMed, Europe PMC or Crossref for this article, so identity rests on the PMID and PMC record (PMC6873135; J Sports Sci Med 2019;18(4):615-622).
implications: Acute cardiac biomarker rise and vagal HRV drop are common after a 118 km race and bigger in faster runners; supports a conservative hold for hard-raced ultras and monitoring sensible warning signs, but gives no day count.
HRV is shown as a readiness tool for racing, not as a validated signal for shortening a post-race hold; do not use this paper to justify wearable-based early release.
